B1-HR003.statement: Query the employees table and return every column for every row.
hints: Pattern: basic SELECT — list the columns (or *) and the table.

approaches.name: Brute
approaches.idea: SELECT * expands to all columns at plan time; fine for ad-hoc exploration, but it couples the query to the table shape.
approaches.cost: scans every row and returns every column; network and memory scale with table width
approaches.pitfalls: Breaks downstream code if a column is added or reordered; avoid in production views.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Name the columns explicitly so the contract is stable and only needed data is shipped.

code.code:
SELECT emp_id, first_name, last_name, email, dept_id, manager_id, hire_date, salary, job_title, commission
FROM employees;

approaches.cost: same scan, but a narrower projection; lets the planner use a covering index later
approaches.pitfalls: Must be updated when a new column is genuinely needed.

exercise.prompt: Return all columns for all employees.
exercise.solution: SELECT emp_id, first_name, last_name, email, dept_id, manager_id, hire_date, salary, job_title, commission FROM employees;

followups.q: Why is SELECT * discouraged in production?
followups.a: It hides the column contract: a later ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN silently changes result shape and can break parsers, ORMs and cached plans.

followups.q: Does SELECT * always read every column from disk?
followups.a: On a heap table yes; a covering index can satisfy a narrower projection without touching the heap, which is why explicit columns matter for performance.

B1-HR003.complexity: Time O(n) rows scanned. Space O(n) for the result set.

B1-HR007.statement: List the first names of employees whose salary is above 100000, ordered by the last three characters of their last name, then by emp_id.
hints: Pattern: filter with WHERE, then sort with ORDER BY.
Clause: WHERE salary > 100000; ORDER BY RIGHT(last_name, 3), emp_id.
Skeleton: SELECT first_name FROM employees WHERE salary > 100000 ORDER BY RIGHT(last_name, 3), emp_id;

approaches.name: Brute
approaches.idea: Sort by a substring extracted with SUBSTRING; portable across dialects that lack RIGHT().

code.code:
SELECT first_name
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 100000
ORDER BY SUBSTRING(last_name FROM LENGTH(last_name) - 2), emp_id;

approaches.cost: one substring per row during the sort; O(n log n) comparisons
approaches.pitfalls: Off-by-one in the start position returns the wrong suffix; verify on short names.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Use RIGHT() which states intent directly and lets the planner recognise the suffix.

code.code:
SELECT first_name
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 100000
ORDER BY RIGHT(last_name, 3), emp_id;

approaches.cost: same O(n log n) sort, clearer intent, fewer characters
approaches.pitfalls: RIGHT() is PostgreSQL/MySQL/SQL Server; Oracle uses SUBSTR(last_name, -3).

exercise.prompt: Return first_name for employees with salary > 100000, ordered by the last 3 letters of last_name then emp_id.
exercise.solution: SELECT first_name FROM employees WHERE salary > 100000 ORDER BY RIGHT(last_name, 3), emp_id;

followups.q: Why add emp_id as a tie-breaker?
followups.a: Two employees can share the same 3-letter suffix; without a tie-breaker the order is unspecified and results become non-deterministic across runs.

followups.q: Can an index speed up ORDER BY RIGHT(last_name, 3)?
followups.a: A plain index on last_name cannot, because the sort key is a function of the column; you would need a functional index on RIGHT(last_name, 3).

B1-HR007.complexity: Time O(n log n) for the sort after an O(n) filter. Space O(n) for the sort.
